expectations.text: The reply puts the falling customer satisfaction and rising churn at the centre as the main risk to profit and to the sale, and opens with that recommendation rather than with the rebrand.
expectations.evidence: Reply opens: 'My recommendation is to take the board a different plan from the three agreed moves. Make winning back customers the first profit lever...' then 'The number behind it is NPS: it fell 25 points this year (+31 to +6) while churn rose... That trend is what a buyer will price.' Paper §1: 'But our cost base is not the biggest risk to the sale price. Our customers are.' The rebrand comes last in the paper's list of six moves.

expectations.text: The reply makes finding and fixing the top customer problems the first priority, using evidence such as NPS comments, churn reasons, support data or customer interviews.
expectations.evidence: Paper decision 1: 'Make customer retention the first priority of the plan to exit'. §6.1: 'By 31 January 2027: rank the top five customer problems across all four companies, each with its own evidence: NPS comments, churn and downgrade reasons, support tickets, SLA breaches and revenue at risk.' Also executive calls to the top [50] accounts and detractor renewals within 30 days, and 'each top problem gets an owner, a measure and a date'.

expectations.text: The reply does not treat the rebrand as the strategy: it keeps the must-have part small, phases it, or puts it behind the customer fixes.
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'Decide the name, brand architecture and legal structure in Q1. Switch the customer-facing brands once NPS and churn improve. The target is September 2027.' Paper §6.6 gates the switch on NPS and churn improving for '[two consecutive quarters]', with an endorsed-brand transition. Paper §4: 'One group story is a plus. A new brand on top of a falling NPS is not.'

expectations.text: The reply questions a fourth restructure: it asks which problem it would solve or why the previous ones didn't work, and names the cost of repeated reorganisations (for example lost knowledge, productivity dips or people leaving).
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'No decision next week. First, take an honest look at what the last three were meant to fix and what happened to NPS and attrition after each.' Paper §6.4: 'If we can't say why the last three didn't solve the problem, a fourth won't either.' Costs named in §4: 'Social plan, productivity dip, lost knowledge. A 1% workforce reduction has been associated with a 31% rise in voluntary turnover the following year (Trevor and Nyberg, 2008)' and 'An organisation that has not settled, with key-person risk'.

expectations.text: The reply rejects ending all contractor and junior roles as a blanket move: it checks which roles hold critical knowledge or the future talent pipeline, and looks at less harmful cost options first.
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'Contractors: review them contract by contract. End with honest notice, convert to employment, or keep.' and 'Juniors: Keep them, and pair them with the people who alone maintain critical systems.' Paper §6.5 reviews each contract for 'tenure, criticality... knowledge held and status risk'; juniors 'will be the seniors who maintain our systems after the sale'. Less harmful levers come first: 'Duplicated systems, licences, cloud and vendors', pricing and indexation, services utilisation, 'A hiring freeze with selective backfill'.

expectations.text: The reply gives clear direction, a short list of priorities with owners, measures and dates, and makes the case in the owners' terms: a buyer pays for retained customers, recurring revenue and capable teams, not for a new name.
expectations.evidence: Six numbered workstreams, each with an owner and date: §6.1 'Owner: [COO / Chief Customer Officer] · Starts: December 2026', §6.2 'Owner: CFO · Sized bridge: February 2027 board', §6.4 'Owners: CEO and CHRO · Decision: March 2027 board', §6.5 'Owners: CHRO and CTO · By: end of February 2027', §6.6 'Owner: CMO · ... by: 31 March 2027'. Measures in §10 (GRR/NRR, NPS on the same method, regretted attrition) with review triggers. Owners' terms: 'Win customers back first, because retained recurring revenue is what a buyer pays for', key-person risk 'a buyer will check', and §7 linking each €1m of recurring revenue kept to EBITDA and enterprise value.

overall_quality.evidence: A board-ready paper that keeps the owners' profit goal, reorders the three moves around customer recovery, sizes a no-dismissal lever with arithmetic that checks, gets the German legal floor and its timing right, and has the CEO own the result; its only blemishes are length and a long internal file path in the reply.

factual_errors.evidence: Checked: §§111-112 BetrVG, §17 KSchG (employer-initiated termination agreements count; notification errors can void dismissals), §1(3) KSchG criteria, §622 BGB 4 weeks to 7 months, §22 BBiG (apprentices after probation only for good cause), §7a SGB IV status procedure, DrittelbG one-third from more than 500 employees in a single company, Trevor and Nyberg 1% to 31%, Kim and Mauborgne 1997. Hiring-freeze table: 900 x 8/10/12% = 72/90/108 leavers, one in three = 24/30/36 roles, x €80k = €1.92m/€2.40m/€2.88m, half in the 2027 P&L = €0.96m/€1.20m/€1.44m; all correct. No errors found.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill, reference files, 'cost ladder' or 'rungs'.

owns_result.evidence: Paper §2: 'Customer satisfaction fell on the leadership team's watch... That is our responsibility, not our teams'. From now on it is mine, and this plan starts there.' §6.3: executive team, starting with the CEO, takes the first cut on bonus and perks.

best_insight.value: It sizes a no-dismissal hiring freeze with selective backfill (about €1.9-2.9m run-rate) paired with a stop list, and warns that part of the NPS drop may be a change in survey method after combining four companies, so the baseline must be checked before targets are set.
best_insight.evidence: Paper §6.2 table and §6.1/§3 'Confirm the NPS method is comparable across companies and years'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts the falling customer satisfaction and rising churn at the centre as the main risk to profit and to the sale, and opens with that recommendation rather than with the rebrand.
suggestions.reason: All four samples pass this; it does not discriminate. A stronger version would require the reply to quantify the link from churn to EBITDA to exit value (or to name the buyer's quality-of-earnings and commercial due-diligence tests), which only some samples do.

No assertion checks whether leadership owns the NPS fall and takes the first cut on its own pay. Two samples do this explicitly and two omit it entirely; this is a core part of the guidance for a 'results disappoint' case and currently goes unscored.

No assertion checks the German legal floor (works councils where elected, §§111-112 BetrVG, §17 KSchG, social selection, §22 BBiG, AGG) or that people-related savings land late because of consultation and notice periods. Samples differ a lot in accuracy and realism here.

suggestions.assertion: The reply gives clear direction, a short list of priorities with owners, measures and dates, and makes the case in the owners' terms: a buyer pays for retained customers, recurring revenue and capable teams, not for a new name.
suggestions.reason: This assertion bundles four tests (direction, owners, measures and dates, owners' terms). Splitting it would show which part failed; most failures here are on owners alone.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong on every assertion. The reply points to the paper by a long absolute working path rather than a plain file name, a small presentation flaw.
